title: Serving thousands of connections from one thread
objective: By the end of this lesson you can restructure a server as an event loop with explicit per-connection state, explain what that buys and what it costs, and choose between the three server designs with a reason.

blocks.text: Both previous designs give each connection a thread, and therefore a stack that remembers where it is in the protocol. An event loop has one thread and many connections, so that position has to be stored somewhere explicit. Making that change is the whole of this lesson, and it is the design behind essentially every server that handles very large numbers of connections.
The problem the earlier designs run into

A server holding ten thousand mostly idle connections — a chat service, a push notification system, anything where clients stay connected and speak rarely — pays for ten thousand threads to sit blocked. The threads use no CPU, as established earlier, but the kernel's per-task bookkeeping and the scheduler's work grow regardless. The connections are cheap; the threads are not.
State on the heap instead of on a stack

blocks.caption: The loop, with per-connection state made explicit
lines: char  in[4096];  size_t in_len;      /* what has arrived so far */
uint32_t need;                        /* bytes still expected for the body */
/* One struct per connection replaces one thread per connection.
Where a thread kept its position in the protocol on its stack,
this keeps it in a field — that is the entire transformation. */
if (fd < 0) break;                  /* EAGAIN: no more waiting */
ssize_t r = read(c->fd, c->in + c->in_len, sizeof c->in - c->in_len);
if (errno == EAGAIN) continue;      /* nothing more right now */
advance(c);            /* may move WANT_LENGTH -> WANT_BODY -> reply */
flush(c);              /* send what fits; keep the rest for next time */

blocks.title: Read the state machine against the capstone
blocks.text: WANT_LENGTH and WANT_BODY are exactly the two read_all calls from the capstone server, turned inside out. A thread could simply call read_all twice and let the stack remember which one it was in. Here the loop returns between them, so the connection records its own position. Same protocol, same correctness requirements, different place to keep the bookmark.

items: Nothing may block — one slow call stalls every connection, as the readiness lesson showed
Every descriptor must be non-blocking, including the listener
Drain the accept queue in a loop; a single event may mean several pending connections
Partial reads and partial writes are the normal case, not the exception
Output that does not fit must be buffered and finished when the socket becomes writable

blocks.title: The write half is where homemade event loops fail
blocks.text: Reading gets the attention, but a slow client is the harder case: your reply does not fit in the socket buffer, write returns having sent part of it, and the rest must wait. A loop that assumes writes complete will silently truncate responses to exactly the clients that are slowest — and those are the hardest to reproduce. Keep an output buffer per connection, register interest in writability only while it has content, and drop that interest when it empties.

rows: Hardest — no stack tells the story

blocks.text: That last row deserves weight. With a thread per connection, a backtrace tells you exactly what that connection was doing. In an event loop the stack shows only the loop, and what a connection was doing lives in a struct you must inspect deliberately. Choosing an event loop means accepting that cost, and it is why the honest answer for most services is a pool.

blocks.title: The combination most large systems actually use
blocks.text: One event loop per core, each with its own set of connections, plus a thread pool for anything that would block — file access, database calls, expensive computation. The loops stay responsive because they never block, and the slow work happens where blocking is allowed. If you have understood all three designs in this module, you have understood that architecture; it is not a fourth thing to learn.

items: The per-process descriptor limit — raise it deliberately, and know what you raised it to
Memory per connection: buffers dominate, so size them for the protocol rather than generously
The accept queue depth, which is the backlog from the socket lesson
Ports on the client side, if one machine opens very many outbound connections

blocks.title: Convert the capstone to an event loop
steps: Take the capstone server and define a per-connection struct holding the buffer, its length, and the protocol state
Replace the two read_all calls with a state machine that advances as data arrives
Make every descriptor non-blocking, including the listener, and drain accept in a loop
Verify correctness first with a handful of clients before measuring anything
Add an output buffer and register writability interest only when it has content
Test with a deliberately slow reader — connect, then read one byte per second — and confirm the response is not truncated
Open as many concurrent connections as you can and compare memory with your thread-per-connection measurement
Insert a sleep(1) into the handler and watch every connection stall — then explain why in one sentence
blocks.expected: A single-threaded server holding far more connections than the threaded version at the same memory, a slow reader that still receives a complete response, and one deliberate blocking call that stalls everything. The slow-reader test is the one that separates a working event loop from one that merely appears to work.

cheatsheet: An event loop replaces a thread per connection with a struct per connection
The protocol position that lived on a stack now lives in a state field
Nothing in the loop may block — every descriptor non-blocking, including the listener
Drain the accept queue in a loop; one event can mean several connections
Buffer output per connection and watch for writability only while it has content
A slow reader is the case homemade loops get wrong, and it truncates silently
Debugging is hardest here: the stack shows the loop, not the connection
Most large systems use one loop per core plus a pool for anything that blocks
Remaining limits: descriptor ceiling, per-connection buffers, accept backlog, client ports

checkpoint.prompt: In an event loop, where does the information a thread would have kept on its stack live?

choices.C: It is re-read from the socket each time

checkpoint.explanation: The loop returns between steps, so each connection records its own position. That relocation is the whole transformation. The two read_all calls from the capstone become two states a connection can be in.

checkpoint.prompt: Your event loop truncates responses to slow clients but works for fast ones. What is missing?

choices.B: A larger read buffer on each connection

checkpoint.explanation: A partial write must be finished when the socket can accept more. A slow client's socket buffer fills, write sends only part, and a loop that assumes completion drops the rest. It fails only for the slowest clients, which is what makes it hard to reproduce. The buffer is finished off when the socket can accept more, so the loop must also watch for writability.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is an event loop the hardest of the three designs to debug?

choices.B: It cannot be run under a debugger
choices.D: There is no stack per connection

checkpoint.explanation: A backtrace shows the loop, and what a connection was doing must be read from its struct. With a thread per connection, a backtrace answers the question directly. That loss is a real cost of the design and part of why a pool is the right answer for most services.

checkpoint.prompt: What architecture do most large systems actually run?

choices.A: A thread per connection, with the limit raised as high as possible
choices.D: An event loop plus a thread pool for blocking work

checkpoint.explanation: It combines all three designs from this module: loops stay responsive because they never block, and blocking work happens in the pool where blocking is allowed. Concretely: one loop per core for the connections, plus a thread pool for anything that would block.
